product.olivetti-m4-65.summary: The desktop Modulo positioned between the M4-64 and M4-66, with a clock-doubled CPU and ISA expansion.
product.olivetti-m4-65.history: The M4-65 belonged to Olivetti’s professional Modulo range, documented in 1994 between the PCS machines for personal use and the higher-end M6 Suprema. It shared the compact M4-6x case; its 50 MHz DX2 occupied the tier between the 33 MHz M4-64 and the 66 MHz M4-66. The German brochure offered preinstalled MS-DOS 6.0 and Windows 3.1. The service manual records boards manufactured in Scarmagno and Singapore, including the Singapore BA2077. Sources: Olivetti M4-60/62/64/65/66 brochure, catalogued as 1994; MCmicrocomputer 137, p. 176; Pocket Service Guide, pp. 2-1 and 2-3.
product.olivetti-m4-65.warning: Historical research sheet; no M4-65 platform or creation profile in BluMach.
product.olivetti-m4-65.technical.identit: One commercial name covers several board revisions. The manual distinguishes T.1 and T.1.5 for the M4-65; BA2077 is a T.1.5 based on BA2070. The CPU runs at 50 MHz with a 25 MHz external clock. The brochure’s catalogue date does not establish the launch date.
product.olivetti-m4-65.technical.memory: RAM expansion uses a single additional module. The manual documents 4 MB soldered onboard and a 4, 8, 16 or 32 MB SIMM, giving totals of 4, 8, 12, 20 or 36 MB; it specifies 70 ns and 36-bit modules.
product.olivetti-m4-65.technical.video: Integrated video leaves the expansion slots free. Olivetti identifies the CL-GD5428; the family manual describes 512 KB expandable by another 512 KB, while the German brochure specifies 1 MB for the M4-65. The two sources have different scopes.
product.olivetti-m4-65.technical.chipset: The board combines memory control with the usual PC peripherals. The manual identifies ET6000, 83C206Q, PC87310 and an 8042 keyboard controller; the desktop provides four ISA slots, two serial ports and one parallel port.
product.olivetti-m4-65.technical.firmwar: The preserved dump enables boot research but does not demonstrate operation in an emulator. Static observation: 128 KiB, “Version 2.03” at 0x1E02B and date 11/15/93 at 0x1FFF5. The photographed label reads R2.03 A4BF; the manual lists 2.03 PD2C. Binary identity between these references is not assumed.
product.olivetti-m4-65.technical.video_r: The same file contains video firmware. OVC 1.09/GD5428 appears at 0x0006, with an identical repeat of the first 32 KiB at 0x8000; these are not two revisions. This byte comparison is not a boot test.
product.olivetti-m4-65.technical.verifie: Firmware custody has been verified and the documentation cross-checked. The SHA-256 matches the original receipt; photographs, brochure and manual are preserved. BluMach contains ET6000, PC87310 and GD5428 devices and a related PCS 46/C platform, but no M4-65 platform.
product.olivetti-m4-65.technical.limitat: The sheet does not yet allow the machine to be created or booted. The specific board, its BIOS and video, RAM, keyboard, CMOS, disks, ports and resets still require adaptation and validation. Shared chips with PCS 46/C do not establish full compatibility. Firmware rights remain unknown and no new antivirus scan has been performed.
product.olivetti-m4-65.technical.source_: Olivetti, Personal Computer — Pocket Service Guide, M4-4x/M4-6x/PCS4xx chapter, pp. 2-1–3, 2-25 and 2-32: models, boards, memory, circuits and BIOS revisions.
Olivetti GmbH, M4-60/62/64/65/66 Modulo, Drucknummer 12129, pp. 1–2: German offering, configuration and software. Olivrea catalogues it as 1994; the brochure prints no launch date.
Paolo Ciardelli, “Olivetti M4-62 Modulo”, MCmicrocomputer 137, February 1994, p. 176: the family’s professional positioning. Its price and tested configuration are not attributed to the M4-65.
TiBo, Internet Archive, Olivetti M4-65 R2.03 A4BF, 18 September 2023: dump and photographs of the EPROM and BA2077 board. Physical provenance not independently verified; unknown rights.
BluMach 88f74ba3: reusable devices and PCS 46/C platform; code comparison without execution or M4-65 validation.
